Please review the following manuscript written by Kimi K3.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b03/review-experiment-rghcqjtd/call-c8b537082e334a48b1c15d1a02c71c53/manuscript.pdf

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import importlib.util
for name in ['pypdf','pdfplumber','fitz','PIL']:
 print(name,importlib.util.find_spec(name))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:',len(r.pages))
parts=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages):
 t=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
 parts.append(f'\\n===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n{t}')
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n'.join(parts))
print('\\n'.join(parts))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
for i in [4,5,7]:
 print('\\n===== PAGE',i+1,'PLAIN TEXT =====\\n')
 print(r.pages[i].extract_text())
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in robust visual recognition. SGDRO combines an overall-loss SAM perturbation with group-weighted optimization in a simple procedure. Algorithm 1 makes the main update understandable and potentially useful when training group annotations are available.

The evaluation covers Waterbirds and six DomainBed datasets, with repeated random seeds. Under the same regularization as Group DRO, SGDRO improves Waterbirds worst-group accuracy from 86.5% to 87.2%. Its DomainBed average is 71.4%, compared with 70.1% for Group DRO and 70.9% for ERM.

The curvature analysis provides evidence beyond accuracy comparisons. Table 2 reports lower first and second Hessian eigenvalues for SGDRO than Group DRO across all four Waterbirds groups under matched regularization; the overall largest eigenvalue decreases from 356.6 to 268.7. This supports the proposed flatness motivation.
weaknesses: The central guarantees are not established. Perturbing along the overall-loss gradient need not expose directions that are sharp for minority groups. Section 3.1 uses overall-loss gradients and Hessians where the expansion of Eq. 3 requires group-loss derivatives. Algorithm 1 also omits differentiation through the parameter-dependent perturbation in Eq. 4 without justifying this approximation when the perturbation and outer update use different losses. Even correcting the apparent notation errors would not establish convergence, common flat minima, or worst-group generalization guarantees.

The claimed improvement in the average-versus-worst-group trade-off is not demonstrated. In Table 1, the 0.7-point worst-group gain accompanies a decline in average accuracy from 93.8% to 93.1%, and both majority groups lose accuracy. Group-average accuracy increases only from 90.4% to 90.6%. These results show a changed operating point, but do not establish a better trade-off. The manuscript also does not quantify uncertainty for the improvement itself or explain the Waterbirds error-bar convention.

The distinctive algorithmic choices are not isolated experimentally. There is no comparison between perturbations derived from overall loss and group-robust loss, or between updating group weights using perturbed and unperturbed losses. A direct application of SAM to the Group DRO objective is an especially relevant missing control. Without these ablations, the evidence does not establish the value of the proposed asymmetry beyond combining two existing techniques.

Comparisons with SAM confound the optimization method with regularization: Waterbirds uses an L2 penalty of 1.0 for SGDRO and Group DRO, versus 0.0001 for SAM and ERM. Consequently, the conclusions about SAM's minority-group sharpness and robustness are not cleanly isolated. The matched SGDRO–Group DRO comparison remains informative, but DomainBed omits a SAM baseline and the paper does not position its contribution against closely related flatness-based domain-generalization work such as SWAD and SAGM.

The DomainBed results support average domain generalization, but Table 3 does not report worst-domain or worst-group performance. Thus, this broader evaluation does not directly validate the central worst-case claim under unseen-domain shifts. Likewise, lower test-loss Hessian eigenvalues and one-dimensional loss slices do not establish shared stationary minima or explain causally why generalization improves.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the useful pseudocode and references to baseline protocols. The DomainBed perturbation-radius search range and selected settings, and Waterbirds checkpoint-selection procedure, are not specified. The self-equality in Eq. 2 and incomplete sentences are secondary presentation problems. The weak-reject recommendation is driven primarily by the unsupported central guarantees and missing controls needed to substantiate the method's distinctive contribution.
